coordination.text: Temple maintenance required water provision, attributed responsibility and written commemoration. A ruler’s image and the practical upkeep of a sanctuary preserve different parts of coordination.

interval.label: Early centuries CE

question: What could a coin communicate?
summary: Kushan coins and temple inscriptions show rulers presenting authority and people carrying out practical work. A coin’s images, an inscription’s account of earlier events and a named well repair have different dates and purposes. Keeping them separate reveals religious patronage and maintenance within a connected region. A royal message could circulate on money, while a sanctuary still needed a dependable water supply and people to build, repair and record it.

sections.title: A small object carried a royal presentation
sections.text: The selected Met gold coin is catalogued around 130 CE and attributed to Gandhara. Its two photographs let us compare figures, attributes and surrounding letters. A ruler chose an image for a monetary object; that is different from documenting everyone’s beliefs. The catalogue’s general description discusses several rulers’ coins, so an example named in that paragraph should not automatically identify this specimen’s reverse. Neither a shared weight convention nor an image proves an individual coin travelled to Rome. Circulation requires find evidence belonging to the particular object.

citations.locator: Date, general coinage paragraph, two views and object details

sections.title: A temple inscription remembered earlier commands
sections.text: At Rabatak, a Bactrian inscription describes royal orders concerning a temple, divine images and images of Kanishka and his predecessors. The account connects kingship with a dynasty and named officials. Sims-Williams distinguishes events assigned to the ruler’s first year from the later creation of the surviving record: possible references to year six make a first-year inscription date unsafe. Translation also preserves uncertain readings. This is evidence for a particular royal commemoration, not a complete map of conquest or a statement that all residents practiced one religion.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 76–78, Rabatak introduction and translation

sections.title: A sanctuary had to be kept supplied
sections.text: The Surkh Kotal inscription describes a water problem and building works begun in year 31 of the Kanishka era, conventionally placed around 158/159 CE. In the translation, Nukunzuk is credited with a well and water provision. A concluding version names Burzmihr in the work and Mihraman as the writer. These names shift attention from royal images to the people through whom a project was carried out and recorded. Some technical terms remain uncertain; the text does not supply a complete engineering plan, payroll or account from every worker.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 78–79, SK 4 and version M

sections.title: Chronology changes the comparison
sections.text: Berlin’s catalogue dates a different Kanishka coin to approximately 127/128–150/151 and explicitly notes disputed dating. The older Met overview uses an earlier reign chronology. This account keeps those sources visible rather than forcing them into one exact accession year. The first-year narrative, the surviving inscription and the selected coin are related kinds of evidence with separate clocks. Peshawar, Mathura and the Bactrian temple region also had distinct local settings; the regional map locates them without inventing imperial borders or the coin’s itinerary.

deeperReading.title: Language and script are different decisions
deeperReading.text: Bactrian is an Iranian language written here using Greek-derived letters. Sims-Williams discusses an uncertain sentence about an edict and a change of language, alongside coin evidence. It should not become an unqualified decree that every subject spoke or read the same language. The Rabatak text’s divine list, royal ancestors and named officials form a specific commemorative setting. The region also supported Buddhist institutions and art, but that wider history is not reducible to one sanctuary or the imagery of one coin. A next inquiry should compare dated local inscriptions and archaeological contexts rather than making every temple a Buddhist monastery.

deeperReading.title: Named builders are visible, but not everyone is
deeperReading.text: The translated Surkh Kotal record attributes actions to an official and preserves additional names in its concluding versions. This is valuable evidence of how work was credited, not proof that the senior official personally performed every task. The document’s copies differ, and terms for the lifting equipment and some titles remain uncertain. A historical explanation can identify water provision as a practical problem while declining to invent the machine’s dimensions or the workers’ legal status. The source also distinguishes the date of the works from the later inscription. Maintenance and commemoration are different actions even when one record connects them.

evidenceReading.title: Keep the event, object and record apart
evidenceReading.introduction: Paraphrases follow the catalogues and Sims-Williams’s translated texts. No new Bactrian transcription is supplied.

items.label: The coin has its own catalogue identity
items.text: Met 99.35.3024 is dated around 130 CE. Berlin 18202384 is a different coin with a broader proposed ruler chronology.
items.interpretation: The Berlin specimen’s weight, deity description or provenance should not be transferred to the Met object. Catalogue attribution is not a documented circulation trail.

items.label: Year one is remembered in a later record
items.text: Rabatak recounts first-year events; its possible year-six reference leads the editor to place the surviving inscription no earlier than around 132/133.
items.interpretation: The statement concerns an interpretation and a lower bound, not an exact carving year. Uncertain words remain marked in the source translation.

items.label: A well connects officials, builders and writing
items.text: Surkh Kotal credits water works under Nukunzuk; version M also names Burzmihr and Mihraman.
items.interpretation: This supports a specific maintenance story. It does not make all work the official’s own manual labor or resolve every technical term.

placeStudy.title: Kushan settings: centers and a temple-inscription region
placeStudy.description: Peshawar and Mathura are approximate city locators. The third point deliberately marks the broader Baghlan temple-inscription region, not exact coordinates of Rabatak, Surkh Kotal or a coin find. No imperial polygon or reconstructed itinerary joins them.

points.label: Peshawar / Purushapura — regional center
points.text: The consulted overview identifies Purushapura, modern Peshawar, as one of Kanishka’s centers. This does not supply a findspot for the selected Met coin.

points.label: Mathura — a different urban setting
points.text: Mathura is named separately in the overview. Connections between political centers do not make their local institutions or communities identical.

points.label: Baghlan region — Rabatak and Surkh Kotal
points.text: Sims-Williams locates the two temple records in this region. The deliberately broad point avoids presenting a speculative modern map coordinate as the precise location of either ancient inscription.
